claims.statement: Tom Allen fired bullets at the Ohio saloon, a rival across the street that had taken his customers.
Tom Allen was in Police Court on a dual charge of disturbing the peace and carrying concealed weapons.
Tom Allen raised a disturbance and fired several shots at The Ohio, a music and beer hall, early on Tuesday 1897-04-27.
Tom Allen was arrested at 2 o'clock on the morning of 1897-04-27 for shooting off a revolver in front of his saloon at Seventh and Market streets (printed as 'in f loon').
Tom Allen was to appear before Judge Peabody on charges of disturbing the peace and a firearms offence; the charge is partly unreadable.
Tom Allen was arrested for discharging his revolver in front of his saloon at Seventh and Market streets, St. Louis.
Tom Allen's case before Judge Peabody was continued until April 30.
Allen's case was continued until April 30 (printed as 'April ov.').
Two cases against Tom Allen were dismissed in Judge Peabody's court on payment of costs.
Tom Allen was to be tried by Judge Peabody on the following Friday.
Tom Allen told his housekeeper, Mrs. Mary Duffy, that a man assaulted across the street the night before had died.
Tom Allen listened to his housekeeper's account of the assault and informed the authorities.
Tom Allen and his housekeeper Mrs. Duffy were summoned before Chief Desmond to tell their stories.
Mrs. Duffy, housekeeper for Tom Allen, was the only witness at the coroner's inquest into the death of William C. Brown who said she saw Brown assaulted.
At first it was reported that Tom Allen had been shot, but the bullet did not hit him.
Several shots were fired during the attack on Tom Allen, but none took effect on him.
